pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Understand SUBTRACTION as taking away / separating from a group to find how many remain. The single most central node in the domain (centrality 0.65) — partner concept to addition-as-combining and the root of all later subtraction work.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving… subtraction (−)…'; 'solve one-step problems that involve… subtraction, using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1/2 represent subtraction and solve take-from problems within 10; take-from (result unknown) is the canonical entry semantics.
• Operational details — Introduce take-away/separate first (remove objects, count what's left), but flag early that subtraction ALSO answers 'how many more/difference' and 'missing part' — these comparison and unknown-part meanings are where children later struggle if only 'take away' is taught. Model the physical removal, narrate it, then count the remainder. Keep within 5-10 with objects the child physically removes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): physically remove some objects and count how many remain. Tier B (age 5): act out a take-from story ('5 biscuits, eat 2') and say how many are left. Tier C (age 5-6): explain subtraction as finding what's left, and recognise a simple 'how many more' difference situation as also being subtraction.
bestPractices: Start with take-away/separate (physically remove and count the remainder) because it is the most concrete meaning, but do NOT stop there — deliberately introduce comparison ('how many more') and missing-part meanings so subtraction isn't permanently equated with 'take away'.
Keep the removed part visible then hidden: showing what was taken and what remains helps the child see the whole splitting into part-taken and part-left (links to part-part-whole).
Narrate action then result ('5 biscuits, take away 2… 3 are left') so 'how many left/remain' attaches to the remaining quantity.
Use the same manipulatives and stories as addition, then contrast: combining makes more, separating leaves fewer — building addition and subtraction as inverse actions from the very start.
Ground the missing-number form (7 = ? − 9 style, or 5 − ? = 3) in acting out, so subtraction-as-unknown-part has an early concrete seed for later formalisation.
keyRepresentations: A group of physical objects with some physically removed/covered (take-away)
Ten-frame with counters removed, remainder visible
Part-part-whole model: whole splits into part-taken and part-left
Two rows of objects lined up for 'how many more' comparison (difference)
Act-out story scenes and drawings with a crossing-out to show removal
commonMisconceptions: Equating subtraction ONLY with 'take away', so comparison ('how many more') and missing-part problems aren't recognised as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.
Trying to 'take away' the larger from the smaller in a comparison and getting confused, or reversing to keep it 'takeable'.
Recounting the whole rather than the remainder, or counting the removed objects instead of what's left.
Believing subtraction always makes a number 'small' and being surprised that 8 − 1 is still large.
Reading 7 − 3 left-to-right as an instruction with no sense that it asks 'how many remain', so missing-number forms feel impossible.

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), build subtraction as taking away / separating from a group to find how many remain — physically removing objects and counting what is left — while deliberately seeding the comparison ('how many more'/difference) and missing-part meanings so subtraction is not permanently equated only with 'take away'. Keep quantities within 5-10 with objects the child physically handles. Introduce take-away first because it is the most concrete meaning, then contrast with addition-as-combining so the two are felt as inverse actions from the start.

activities.title: Take-away mat: remove and read what's left
feedback: If the child reports 2 (how many eaten): physically separate the 2, then point to the remaining group and ask 'how many are LEFT?'; name the difference between the result and the action.
If the child answers 7 (adds the numbers): act the story out — start with 5 and physically take 2 away — so the situation, not the two numbers, drives the operation.

If the child recounts the whole remaining set slowly from one instead of counting back: accept it. Let them recount the remainder; counting-back matures later and slow recounting is not an error here.
Probe: 'Show me with the biscuits what eating 2 does to the pile.' 'Which biscuits are the answer — the ones you ate or the ones still there?'
activities.rationale: Take-away/separate is the most concrete entry meaning; letting the child perform the removal and attend to the remainder targets the common errors of reporting the amount taken, reporting the original whole instead of what is left, or adding. Keeping the removed part briefly visible then hidden helps the child see the whole splitting into part-taken and part-left (part-part-whole).
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent subtraction with objects/drawings and solve take-from word problems within 10.
Y1 pupils read/write/interpret statements involving − and solve one-step subtraction and missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = ? − 9) with concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Start with 5 biscuits on a plate; physically remove (drag/take) 2 into a bin.
Watch or track the remaining count fall as you remove: 5 → 4 → 3.
Say and, if ready, assemble the statement '5 − 2 = 3'.
Point to which biscuits are the answer — the ones still on the plate, not the ones taken.
Narrate the action then the result: '5 biscuits, take away 2… 3 are left.'
activities.intendedInsight: The starting group splits into 'gone' and 'left', and the answer to a take-away is what remains — subtraction felt as a physical removal, with 'how many left' attached to the remaining quantity.

activities.title: Difference mode: 'how many more?' as subtraction
feedback: If the child tries to 'take away' the larger from the smaller or reverses the rows to keep it 'takeable': re-align the two rows one-to-one and point only to the unmatched tail as the answer.
Reinforce by lining the rows up physically so the matched pairs and the leftover tail are visually clear.
activities.rationale: Comparison and missing-part meanings are where children later struggle if only 'take away' is taught; aligning two rows makes the difference visible and concrete. This extends, rather than replaces, the take-away activity.
sourceClaims: Subtraction should be taught across take-away, comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings, not take-away alone, to prevent long-run difficulty.
learnerActions: Line up two rows of objects, one under the other, matching them one-to-one.
Find the unmatched tail — the objects in the longer row with no partner.
Count that leftover tail to answer 'how many more does this row have?'
Connect it back: this 'how many more' is also a subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction also answers comparison/difference questions ('how many more'), not only 'take away'. Meeting difference early is intended to help prevent the long-run difficulty of not recognising comparison problems as subtraction.

activities.title: Mystery removed: reason back to the missing part
feedback: If the child is stuck, let them act it out with real objects: start from the whole, remove groups, and check which removal leaves the remaining amount.
Keep the missing-number idea grounded in action rather than as abstract symbol manipulation at this age.
activities.rationale: Grounding the missing-number form in acting out gives subtraction-as-unknown-part an early concrete seed for later formalisation and links to inverse/unknown-addend thinking; it also addresses the misconception that a subtraction statement is just an instruction to perform rather than a relationship between a whole and its parts, where any one part can be the unknown.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils read/write/interpret statements involving − and solve one-step subtraction and missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = ? − 9) with concrete objects and pictorial representations.
Subtraction should be taught across take-away, comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings, not take-away alone, to prevent long-run difficulty.
learnerActions: See the starting group (e.g. 5) and the remaining group (e.g. 3), with the taken pile hidden or covered.
Work out how many must have been removed to leave what's there.
Act out or check by uncovering the hidden pile.
Say it as a missing-part sentence, e.g. '5 − ? = 3'.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction can ask for the unknown part that was taken away — an early concrete seed for missing-number forms (e.g. 5 − ? = 3, or 3 = 5 − ?) and for subtraction-and-addition as inverse actions. Acting it out also counters reading a written statement as a bare left-to-right instruction with no sense of the quantities involved.

activities.title: Still-scene anchor and take-from stories
feedback: Use the scene to confirm the remainder, but move to objects the child removes so they perform the action rather than only recognise the aftermath.
When talking, keep real objects present so reasoning is grounded, not reliant on still-forming language alone.
Ask: 'If you ate 3 instead of 2, would more or fewer be left? Why?' 'A friend says 5 take away 2 is 7 — what would you tell them?'
activities.rationale: A static crossed-out scene and tap-to-reveal anchor the take-away meaning and are useful supports; spoken co-play surfaces reasoning. These are anchors/scaffolds rather than the primary builder because the concept is about acting on objects, and recognising a revealed answer does not itself elicit the child's own removal.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent subtraction with objects/drawings and solve take-from word problems within 10.
learnerActions: Look at a take-from scene (e.g. 5 biscuits, 2 with a bite taken or crossed out) and tap/lift a flap to reveal 'how many left?'.
Act out take-from stories aloud with real objects: '5 biscuits, eat 2 — how many are left?'
Alongside a parent or partner, talk through 'we ate some — how many are left?' while handling the actual objects.
Use the same manipulatives and stories used for addition, then contrast: combining makes more, separating leaves fewer.
activities.intendedInsight: A still take-from picture and spoken stories anchor the take-away meaning and language; contrasting with addition builds subtraction and addition as inverse actions.

constraints: Keep quantities within 5-10 and use objects the child can physically remove.

Do not stop at 'take away': deliberately introduce comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings. The evidence base identifies that if only 'take away' is taught, children tend to stop recognising comparison and missing-part problems as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.

A still take-from picture (crossed-out/bite scene with tap-to-reveal) anchors the take-away meaning but does not let the child perform the removal or explore comparison/missing-part meanings; treat it as a scaffold, not the sole teacher.

Talk-only prompts lean on still-forming language at this age; pair any 'how many are left?' conversation with real objects rather than using it alone. This does not mean talk cannot support reasoning.
Do not insist on counting-back or mark slow recounting of the remainder as wrong; counting-back matures later. Removing objects and recounting the remainder is acceptable.

Scored, linear picture quizzes are developmentally weak for ages 4-6; a small picture item may check recognition of 'how many left' but does not itself elicit the child's own physical removal, so keep any such item minor and not the primary route for building the concept.

Watch for 'subtraction always makes a number small': show that taking away leaves fewer than the start but not necessarily a small amount (e.g. 8 − 1 = 7, still a lot), so the child isn't surprised by it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three listed sources, the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified; the Common Core (K.OA) and NCETM/CGI comparison-structures claims are marked unverified in the source row — the comparative/structural guidance they support (including the 'guards against long-run difficulty' rationale) should be treated as informed practice, not confirmed efficacy.

The 'live remainder counter' and automatic sentence assembly are optional interaction examples that make the removal mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory. The core learning works with any physically removable objects.

Original row framed a static image as showing 'only the aftermath' and 3D as adding 'nothing'/only handling cost; these are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims, and are not asserted here. A still scene can still anchor the meaning; different media simply offer different experiences.
The audit retains the genuine objective limit that still pictures and recognition/reveal formats do not elicit the child's own physical removal, without claiming any medium is universally necessary.

The original misconception of reading a subtraction statement as a bare left-to-right instruction (so missing-number forms feel impossible) is addressed explicitly in the 'mystery removed' activity by grounding the symbolic form in acting out.

probeDeeper: Show me with the biscuits what 'eating 2' does to the pile.
If you ate 3 instead of 2, would more or fewer be left? Why?
Which biscuits are the answer — the ones you ate or the ones still there?
A friend says 5 take away 2 is 7. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 — by removing 2 from the 5 and attending to what REMAINS (counting the leftover, or counting back 5 → 4 → 3), not by counting the ones taken away or by combining.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the amount TAKEN AWAY (2) instead of what is left — attends to the action, not the result.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically separate the 2, then draw attention to the remaining group and ask 'how many are LEFT'; label result vs action.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 2 and points to the eaten biscuits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back from one / recounts the whole set rather than counting back, or loses track counting back.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT insist on counting-back or mark slow recounting as wrong — remove the objects and let the child recount the remainder; counting-back matures later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child recounts the remaining biscuits slowly from one, or cannot count back reliably.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two numbers instead of taking away — treats any two quantities as 'put together'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act the story out — start with 5, physically take 2 away — so the situation drives the operation rather than the numbers.

responseLevels.gap: Reports the amount taken away, or adds the numbers, or cannot find what remains.
responseLevels.full: Removes the part and reads the remainder (or counts back), and explains subtraction as finding how many are left.
responseLevels.partial: Finds 3 by physically removing and recounting the whole set from one; take-away enacted but not yet counting back or recalling.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You have 5 biscuits and you eat 2 of them. How many biscuits are left? How do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands subtraction as taking away removes 2 and focuses on the remainder; a child who does not may report how many were eaten (2), add the numbers (7), or lose track. The reason reveals whether 'take away' is understood as separating a part and reading the rest.
